items.title: Al Rose Interview, 1975-02-19
items.q: I think that it's interesting that Duke Ellington has developed the reputation that he has... he was not, in fact, a composer

ctx.x: You have a completely different view of Duke Ellington. That's true. Can you just explain a little bit? Yeah, well. I think it's interesting.

Well, I think that it's interesting that Duke Ellington has developed the reputation that he has. Really, it's an indictment of the criteria of the American public that he is accepted as being a great musical genius. One thing is, of course, that so far as I am able to determine on the basis of what I would consider to be reasonable investigation, first, that he was not, in fact, a composer, that he never really composed anything at all of any significance, certainly none of the things with which his name is…
Jimmy Noon's solo became the Creole Love Call. Yes. Jimmy Noon's solo in one of the King Oliver pieces.

items.title: Al Rose Interview, 1975-02-19
items.q: Take the A train, says Hodges Ellington. This is all true. But what I'm saying is that in none of these cases did Ellington make any contribution to the composition.

ctx.x: Or that his name appears with Barney Begard's on Mood Indigo, which Barney Begard had nothing to do with the composition of that either. Take the A train, says Hodges Ellington. This is all true. But what I'm saying is that in none of these cases did Ellington make any contribution to the composition. These were all compositions of these various people. Now, because of slick publicity, he has been presented as a great creative genius who has composed all these pieces.
But it's not just slick publicity, Al. It's people like Gunther Schuller who in their book, Early Jazz, call him the first great composer.
